name: Fatima Gupta

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work on Greenbank, my husband's family farm. It's a hundred and twenty hectares with beef cattle, a flock of sheep, potatoes, and a farm shop at the end of the lane, and the shop is mostly mine. A normal day, I open at nine, set out the eggs, the potatoes, the cakes from the lady in the village, serve until two, and then I'm out helping Sanjay, my husband's brother, with whatever needs doing on the farm.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: You came to the farm later in life?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Three years ago. I was a teaching assistant at the primary school for twenty-five years. When the woman who ran the shop retired, Sanjay asked if I'd take it on, and Ravi, my husband, said family should keep it in the family. I knew how to talk to children and parents, but I didn't know a heifer from a bullock.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the shop. It's like the school gate, everybody tells you everything while they wait for change. What wears me out is the farm side, the potato harvest especially, standing on the picking machine taking stones out for ten hours. And the shop accounts. Sanjay looks at my figures and sighs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. Here's the first picture. Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's useful for some things. My niece Zara showed me how to ask it to write the shop's Facebook posts, and now people say how nice they are. I'd say don't be frightened of it, but don't believe everything it says either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it helps me a little and doesn't change anything that matters. The shop is about people. Nobody comes down our lane because of a clever post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different. Keep about three months saved, which Ravi is very strict about. Maybe ask Zara to show me how to use it for the shop accounts, because Sanjay's sighing is getting louder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like getting a better till.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about one of those Facebook posts.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I told it, write something about our new-season potatoes, friendly, short. It wrote that our potatoes were kissed by the morning dew. Ravi laughed so much he had to sit down, so I changed it to just say they're good for roasting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said it's about people. What do people actually come for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: People don't drive twenty minutes down a muddy lane for eggs. They come for a chat with someone who knows their mother's name. Old Mr Hughes comes in every Tuesday for six eggs and stays forty minutes.

S0.say: I'd say it's useful for some things, like writing the shop's Facebook posts with my niece's help. Don't be frightened of it, but don't believe everything it says either.
S0.think: Privately it helps me a little and doesn't change what matters, because the shop is about people. Nobody comes down our lane because of a clever post.
S0.do: Keeps about three months of savings, as her husband insists. Asks her niece to show her how to use AI for the shop accounts.
S0.feel: Calm, like getting a better till.
S0.quote: It wrote that our potatoes were kissed by the morning dew.
S0.fieldNote: Fatima uses AI the way she'd use any new gadget, carefully and with family help. She's very clear that the shop runs on relationships. Her family runs through every answer: husband, brother-in-law, niece.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thank you. Second picture. Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say family farms have always trained their own, so we'll be fine. It's the big companies that'll stop taking beginners. I'd say young people should learn a trade from their families and neighbours, the old way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'm a beginner on our own farm, and I only got in because I'm family. If nobody hires beginners, then family is the only way in, and lots of young people don't have a farm in the family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Sanjay to teach me more of the stock work, properly, so I'm not just the shop lady. I'd take on a Saturday girl in the shop, a schoolgirl, and teach her what I know. And I'd keep the savings where they are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A little sad for young people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would the Saturday girl be?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably Leila, from the mosque, she's fifteen and very sharp with numbers. Her mother's asked me twice. She'd learn the till, the customers, and to smile when Mr Hughes tells the same story.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said family farms train their own. What about young people without a family farm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the hard part, and I don't have a good answer. Maybe farms like ours should take one young person each, not because the government tells us, but because it's right. My father always said, you leave the ladder down for the next one.

S1.say: I'd say family farms have always trained their own and it's the big companies that'll stop taking beginners. Young people should learn a trade from family and neighbours.
S1.think: I only got in as a beginner because I'm family. If nobody hires beginners, family is the only way in, and many young people don't have that.
S1.do: Asks Sanjay to teach her stock work properly and takes on a Saturday schoolgirl in the shop to train. Keeps savings where they are.
S1.feel: Calm, with some sadness for young people.
S1.quote: My father always said, you leave the ladder down for the next one.
S1.fieldNote: She saw the unfairness in her own luck and didn't hide it. Her answer is traditional: farms taking young people on out of duty, not because the state tells them. The Saturday girl is a small, real plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. Here's the third. Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people should work hard and retrain, and the government should help them do it, not just pay them to stay home. Families have to pull together. I'd say that in the shop, because everybody talks about it there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my daughter Aisha works in human resources at a big supermarket's head office, sorting staff contracts and pay questions. That's routine office work, isn't it. She's thirty-two, and she's just bought a house with her husband.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Aisha to start learning something hands-on in the evenings, maybe bookkeeping for small firms, or even come and help with the shop's marketing. I'd move some of our savings into an account she could use if needed. And I'd keep the shop prices steady, because people will be counting their pennies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Worried for Aisha, and for my customers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said bookkeeping. Isn't that office work too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, you're right, I said that without thinking. Maybe the point is she should do it for people she knows, like the farms round here. People trust a face, even with numbers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which customers would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's a young couple, the Okafors, both work in offices in the city, they come Saturdays with their baby. They buy the expensive sausages. I'd notice the day they switched to the cheap ones, and I wouldn't say a word, I'd just slip an extra one in the bag.

S2.say: I'd say people should work hard and retrain, and the government should help with that rather than paying people to stay home. Families have to pull together.
S2.think: Privately I'd worry about my daughter Aisha, who handles staff contracts at a supermarket head office. She's thirty-two and has just bought a house.
S2.do: Encourages Aisha to learn a practical skill in the evenings or help with the shop's marketing and sets aside savings she can use. Keeps shop prices steady for customers counting pennies.
S2.feel: Uneasy for her daughter and her customers.
S2.quote: I'd notice the day they switched to the cheap ones, and I wouldn't say a word, I'd just slip an extra one in the bag.
S2.fieldNote: She recommended bookkeeping and then caught that it's office work too, landing on the idea that people trust a face. Her care for customers is quiet and practical. Family and the shop are her two worlds, and both get her attention here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thank you. The fourth one is faster. Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the people doing well should look after their own communities, give to the food bank, buy local, pay their workers fairly. I don't think a fight in parliament will feed anybody. I'd say it to anyone in the shop who brought it up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, the shop might do very well. People with booming shares and houses buy the expensive cheese and the hampers at Christmas. But half my regulars are office people, and they'd be losing their jobs, so I'd be selling hampers to some and slipping sausages to others.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to Sanjay about a cheaper range in the shop, eggs, potatoes, soup bones, for people who are struggling. I'd give more to the mosque food bank. And Aisha and her husband could move in with us for a while if they had to, we have the room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Busy and worried, both at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a fight in parliament won't feed anybody. Should the government do nothing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not nothing. They should help people find work and keep the small businesses going. But a food bank run by neighbours knows who's hungry better than any office in the capital.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Physical jobs are untouched here. Does the farm feel safe?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The farm, yes. The cattle and the potatoes don't care about the share price. It's the shop I'd watch, because the shop lives on people's spare money.

S3.say: I'd say the people doing well should look after their communities by giving to the food bank, buying local and paying fairly. A fight in parliament won't feed anybody.
S3.think: I think the shop might do well selling expensive cheese and hampers to people getting rich. But half my regulars are office people losing their jobs.
S3.do: Talks to Sanjay about a cheaper range for struggling customers and gives more to the mosque food bank. Offers Aisha and her husband a room if they need it.
S3.feel: Uneasy; busy and worried at the same time.
S3.quote: I'd be selling hampers to some and slipping sausages to others.
S3.fieldNote: She saw the boom splitting her own customers into two groups and planned for both. Her traditional view puts neighbours and the food bank ahead of government, but she isn't against all help. The shop, not the farm, is where she feels the change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. This is the last one. Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we must be careful. Machines can help on a farm, but a family farm is a family, not a factory. I'd say people should support local shops and local workers, and I'd say it louder than before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, the farm side would change a lot. Sanjay would probably buy a robot for the potato harvest, and that's the work I do worst, so maybe it's a mercy. But robots in shops and kitchens too, that's the bit that frightens me, because the shop is my real job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait and see what other farm shops do, and learn from the ones that keep their customers. I'd make the shop more of a place to stop, put in two tables and sell tea, because a robot can't sit with Mr Hughes. And I'd keep four months saved, not three.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not panicked, because family is family, but anxious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the robot took the potato picking, would you miss it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My back wouldn't. But I'd miss the jokes on the picking machine, Sanjay's terrible singing, the radio. A robot doesn't sing badly, and that's part of why it's lonely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said family is family. Would Sanjay ever let you go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He wouldn't let me go, but he might ask me to do less, and pay me less, if the shop wasn't paying its way. And that's fair, I believe in a business earning its keep. I'd just have to make sure it did.

S4.say: I'd say we must be careful, because a family farm is a family, not a factory. People should support local shops and local workers, and I'd say it louder than before.
S4.think: I think Sanjay would probably buy a potato harvest robot, and that's the work I do worst. Robots in shops and kitchens frighten me more, because the shop is my real job.
S4.do: Waits to see what other farm shops do and learns from those that keep customers. Adds two tables and tea to make the shop a place to stop, and builds savings from three months to four.
S4.feel: Anxious but not panicked, because family stands behind her.
S4.quote: A robot doesn't sing badly, and that's part of why it's lonely.
S4.fieldNote: She'd lose the farm work she does worst and admits that might be a mercy. Her real fear is for the shop, and her answer is to make it more human, not more efficient. She accepts the free-market rule that the shop must earn its keep, even for family.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The last one, because of the shop. What would help is people choosing to buy from people, and maybe lower business rates, the local tax on shops, for small places that employ local folk. And courses for people like me on running a small business, near home, in the evenings.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the old people who come in. For some of them, I'm the only person they talk to all week. If the shop goes, that goes too, and nobody will count it.

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Thank you. Take some eggs, they're from this morning.

headlineQuote: People don't drive twenty minutes down a muddy lane for eggs. They come for a chat with someone who knows their mother's name.
portrait: Fatima is a 58-year-old former teaching assistant who now runs the farm shop on her husband's family farm and helps, still clumsily, with the cattle and potatoes. She is traditional, puts family, faith and neighbours first, and uses AI now and then for the shop's posts with her niece's help. As the scenarios speed up, she worries for her daughter's office job and for customers being split between those getting rich and those losing work. With robots, she'd gladly lose the potato picking but fears for the shop, and plans to make it more human.
biggestWorry: The robot picture worries her most, because robots in shops and kitchens threaten the farm shop that is her real job.
whatWouldHelp: People choosing to buy from people, lower business rates for small local employers, and evening courses near home on running a small business.
